title: Black touring shows: Butterbeans and Suzie, Ida Cox, Ethel Waters
summary: Jones recalls meeting Butterbeans and Suzie in Birmingham and describes the big black acts, Eddie Lemons, Ida Cox, and the record Hinton and he made with her.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: You just mentioned Ethel Waters and Ma Rainey had a show. These were black shows... We just want it for the records so that the reader and the listener will know that these were great shows - and the Whitman Sisters -

I met in 1923, I met Butterbeans and Suzie and I was running errands and getting their food at the Frolic Theatre in Birmingham, Alabama. That's authenticated and truthfully. Everything that is really in show business, and Miller and Lyles and all that.

It's no way in the world that Eddie Lemons and his Dashing Dinah Revue show - these people had cars, they had 7 or 8 cars on the railroad that had their names on it. That was a big black act. Miss Ida Cox, which she was on a recording, when she came in she still had her diamonds and only had about 80 homes in Knoxville.
Hey, you and I made that record.
We did with Coleman Hawkins and Roy Eldridge.
We want to pull that out and we'll take an intermission.
With Roy Eldridge and Sammy Price.

And she still had the same authentic diamonds that she always had. They didn't find her washing dishes at Macy's. And Butterbeans and Susie, when they bought their home in Chicago anyone could come to that, anyone who was in the profession. When Miss Ethel Waters, before she went into "As Thousands Cheer" to tour all over, when she came out with the great bandleader Leroy Smith, when she had that show she didn't have no money -
Leroy Smith, as far as I know he was an eastern black.
Because I only got a chance to see it once.
